ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure is a circuit, with a parallel-plate capacitor C on the left, two horizontal plates separated by d; between the plates there is a dashed interface, labeled as d/3 from the lower plate, indicating the initial liquid level height. On the right is connected a resistor R, and the whole forms an RC circuit. Reasoning: The liquid thickness decreases with time as h(t)=d/3-Vt. Since the liquid layer and the air layer are distributed vertically along the electric field direction, they should be equivalent to two parallel-plate capacitors in series: liquid layer thickness h, dielectric constant K=2; air layer thickness d-h, dielectric constant approximately 1. The plate area is 1, so \frac{1}{C(t)}=\frac{h}{K\epsilon_0}+\frac{d-h}{\epsilon_0}. Substituting K=2: \frac{1}{C(t)}=\frac{h}{2\epsilon_0}+\frac{d-h}{\epsilon_0}=\frac{d-h/2}{\epsilon_0}. Then substituting h=d/3-Vt: d-\frac{h}{2}=d-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{d}{3}-Vt\right)=\frac{5d}{6}+\frac{Vt}{2}=\frac{5d+3Vt}{6}. Therefore C(t)=\frac{6\epsilon_0}{5d+3Vt}. The RC time constant is \tau(t)=RC(t), so \tau(t)=\frac{6\epsilon_0R}{5d+3Vt}.

method.method_draft: First read the diagram as a parallel-plate capacitor connected to a resistor R, with horizontal plates separated by d and a dashed liquid-air interface initially at height d/3 above the lower plate. Let the liquid thickness at time t be h(t)=d/3 - Vt. Since the liquid and air occupy layers along the electric-field direction, model the capacitor as two capacitors in series: a liquid-filled slab of thickness h and dielectric constant K=2, and an air slab of thickness d-h. For unit plate area, use 1/C = h/(K epsilon_0) + (d-h)/epsilon_0. Substitute K=2 and h=d/3 - Vt to get C(t)=6 epsilon_0/(5d+3Vt). Then use the RC time constant tau(t)=R C(t), giving tau(t)=6 epsilon_0 R/(5d+3Vt).

Therefore
C(t)=\frac{6\epsilon_0}{5d+3Vt}.
The RC time constant is \tau(t)=RC(t), so
\tau(t)=\frac{6\epsilon_0R}{5d+3Vt}.
